items.task: Calculate the amounts that should be included in an individual's gross income (wages, interest, dividends, guaranteed payments, fringe benefits, retirement plan income, punitive damages).
items.stem: Two taxpayers, both age 63, each took a $20,000 distribution from an IRA in 2026, and neither owes a required minimum distribution. Ana's distribution came from a traditional IRA funded entirely with deductible contributions. Ben's came from a Roth IRA that he opened eight years ago and funded entirely with after-tax contributions of $12,000, plus earnings. Which statement correctly compares the amounts included in their 2026 gross income?
options: Ana includes $20,000 and Ben includes $8,000, the earnings in excess of his contributions
Ana and Ben each include $20,000, because IRA distributions are taxable when withdrawn
Neither includes any amount, because both are older than age 59 1/2
Ana includes $20,000 and Ben includes $0, because his distribution is a qualified Roth distribution

why.A: Applies the ordering rule for nonqualified Roth distributions (contributions first, then earnings). Ben's distribution is qualified, so that rule does not apply.
why.B: Treats a Roth IRA like a traditional IRA. Qualified Roth distributions are not included in gross income.
why.C: Age 59 1/2 only removes the 10 percent additional tax. Ana's deductible contributions and earnings have never been taxed, so her distribution is included.
why.D: A qualified Roth distribution (made after age 59 1/2 and after the five-year period) is entirely excluded, earnings included. Ana's traditional IRA has no basis, so the whole $20,000 is taxable.

items.law_note: Unchanged by OBBBA; no phase-out or dollar limits are used.

items.task: Review Form 1040 and supporting documentation to determine completeness and accuracy of gross income reported.
items.stem: Review the exhibit for Grace Holt's 2026 return. Grace is single and reports all $3,000 of dividends from her Forms 1099-DIV as qualified dividends. Which correction is required?
options: Report $1,800 as qualified dividends, because stock must be owned more than 60 days before the ex-dividend date
Report $1,800 as qualified dividends; the Gamma Corp. dividend fails because she bought it fewer than 60 days before the ex-dividend date
No correction is required, because all three payers are domestic corporations
Report $2,200 as qualified dividends; the Beta Inc. dividend fails the holding period requirement and is an ordinary dividend

why.A: Misreads the rule. The 60 days are counted within the 121-day window around the ex-dividend date and need not precede it. That reading wrongly disqualifies Alpha and Gamma.
why.B: Gamma was bought 28 days before the ex-dividend date, but she kept it through year end, so the days held inside the 121-day window exceed 60. Gamma qualifies, and the $1,200 stays qualified.
why.C: A domestic payer is necessary but not enough. The taxpayer must also satisfy the holding period for each stock, and Beta fails it.
why.D: Grace held Beta only 26 days, fewer than the required more than 60 days during the 121-day period that begins 60 days before the ex-dividend date. Alpha and Gamma were held long enough.

steps: Beta: acquired May 10, sold June 5; days held (excluding acquisition day, including sale day) = 21 + 5 = 26, fewer than 61
Alpha and Gamma held through year end, more than 60 days in each 121-day window

items.task: Calculate the capital gain included in gross income from sale of investments/virtual currency, gifts and inherited assets; classify as long-term or short-term.
items.stem: Priscilla Lund sold land she held as an investment for many years for $300,000 in 2026. Her adjusted basis was $120,000. The buyer paid $60,000 at closing and gave a note for the remaining $240,000, payable in equal annual installments over the next four years, beginning in 2027, with adequate stated interest. Compare the gain Priscilla reports in 2026 if she uses the installment method with the gain she reports if she elects out of it. Which statement is correct?
options: $36,000 under the installment method; $180,000 if she elects out
$60,000 under the installment method; $180,000 if she elects out
$36,000 under the installment method; $60,000 if she elects out
$24,000 under the installment method; $180,000 if she elects out

why.A: Gross profit percentage = $180,000 / $300,000 = 60%. Payments received in 2026 of $60,000 x 60% = $36,000. Electing out reports the whole $180,000 gain in the year of sale.
why.B: Treats the entire down payment as gain. Under the installment method each payment is part recovery of basis and part gain.
why.C: Limits the elect-out gain to cash received. Electing out means the note is treated as payment and the full gain is reported in 2026.
why.D: Applies the basis percentage (40%) to the down payment instead of the gross profit percentage (60%).

items.law_note: Unchanged by OBBBA. Land held for investment: no depreciation recapture.

items.task: Calculate the amounts that should be included in an individual's gross income (wages, interest, dividends, guaranteed payments, fringe benefits, retirement plan income, punitive damages).
items.stem: In 2026 Dara Nunn received 1,000 shares of her employer's stock for her services, paying $2,000 for them. The shares are subject to a substantial risk of forfeiture and vest on June 1, 2028. The shares were worth $10,000 when granted in 2026 and are worth $50,000 at vesting. Compare the compensation income Dara reports if she makes a timely election to include the value of the stock in income when she receives it with the income she reports if she makes no election. Which statement is correct?
options: With the election, $10,000 in 2026; without it, $50,000 at vesting in 2028
With the election, $8,000 in 2026 and another $40,000 at vesting; without it, $48,000 at vesting
With the election, nothing in 2026 because the shares are unvested; without it, $48,000 at vesting
With the election, $8,000 in 2026 and no compensation at vesting; without it, $48,000 at vesting in 2028

why.A: Ignores the $2,000 Dara paid for the shares. Compensation is the value less the amount paid.
why.B: Taxes the appreciation as compensation even with the election. After a valid election, later appreciation is not compensation.
why.C: Describes the result when no election is made. The election is what causes inclusion in the year of transfer.
why.D: With the election, income equals the grant-date value less the amount paid: $10,000 - $2,000 = $8,000, and later appreciation is capital gain. Without it, income is measured at vesting: $50,000 - $2,000 = $48,000.

steps: Election: FMV at transfer 10,000 - amount paid 2,000 = 8,000 in 2026
No election: FMV at vesting 50,000 - amount paid 2,000 = 48,000 in 2028

items.task: Calculate the capital gain included in gross income from sale of investments/virtual currency, gifts and inherited assets; classify as long-term or short-term.
items.stem: As part of their 2026 divorce, Kim Ostrow transferred to her former spouse Lee, under the divorce instrument, 500 shares of stock she bought years ago for $20,000. The shares were worth $70,000 on the transfer date. Lee sold them later in 2026 for $90,000. Separately, Kim sold 500 identical shares (also with a $20,000 basis) to an unrelated buyer for $70,000. Which statement correctly compares the gain recognized?
options: Kim recognizes no gain on the transfer to Lee and a $50,000 gain on the sale to the buyer; Lee recognizes a $70,000 gain
Kim recognizes no gain on the transfer to Lee and a $50,000 gain on the sale to the buyer; Lee recognizes a $20,000 gain
Kim recognizes a $50,000 gain on both the transfer and the sale; Lee recognizes a $20,000 gain
Kim recognizes a $50,000 gain on both the transfer and the sale; Lee recognizes a $70,000 gain

why.A: A transfer between spouses incident to divorce is not a taxable event and Lee takes Kim's $20,000 basis: $90,000 - $20,000 = $70,000. The sale to the unrelated buyer is taxable: $70,000 - $20,000 = $50,000.
why.B: Gives Lee a $70,000 fair market value basis. Property received in a divorce transfer keeps the transferor's basis.
why.C: Treats the divorce transfer as a sale at fair market value and gives Lee a stepped-up basis. Neither applies to a transfer incident to divorce.
why.D: Taxes Kim on the divorce transfer while still using her carryover basis for Lee. Kim has no gain on a transfer incident to divorce.

steps: Transfer to Lee: no gain or loss to Kim; Lee's basis = 20,000

items.task: Calculate the amounts that should be included in an individual's gross income (wages, interest, dividends, guaranteed payments, fringe benefits, retirement plan income, punitive damages).
items.stem: In 2026 Mira Vaughn and Noel Ames, both single, each received a $3,000 refund of state income tax paid for 2025. Both itemized deductions on their 2025 returns; neither was affected by the annual limit on state and local taxes. Mira's 2025 itemized deductions were $22,000 and Noel's were $16,500. The 2025 standard deduction for a single filer was $15,750. Which statement correctly states the refund each includes in 2026 gross income?
options: Mira and Noel each include $3,000, because every state tax refund is taxable
Neither includes any refund, because state taxes are not income
Mira includes $6,250 and Noel includes $750
Mira includes $3,000 and Noel includes $750

why.A: Includes the full refund without testing whether the deduction produced a tax benefit. Noel benefited by only $750.
why.B: The refund recovers an amount previously deducted and is included to the extent of the prior benefit.
why.C: Uses each taxpayer's full excess of itemized deductions over the standard deduction. The inclusion cannot exceed the $3,000 refund.
why.D: A refund is income only to the extent the earlier deduction reduced tax. Mira's itemized excess over the standard deduction, $6,250, exceeds the refund, so all $3,000 is included. Noel's excess is $16,500 - $15,750 = $750.

items.law_note: Unchanged by OBBBA; the stem supplies the 2025 standard deduction (raised for 2025 by OBBBA).

items.stem: Review the exhibit for Cole Rivera's 2026 Schedule E. Cole is a cash-basis landlord. His draft return reports $18,000 of rents received. What amount of rental income should the return report?
exhibit: Monthly rent for January through December 2026
Payment on December 20, 2026 for January 2027 rent
Security deposit, refundable at lease end, held in the landlord's bank account
Payment from a departing tenant to cancel a lease

why.A: Leaves out the $2,000 lease cancellation payment, which is treated as rent when received.
why.B: Leaves out the December payment for January 2027 rent. Advance rent is included when received.
why.C: Cole includes all rent received in 2026 regardless of the period it covers: $18,000 + $1,500 of advance rent + $2,000 lease cancellation payment = $21,500. A refundable security deposit is not income until it is kept.
why.D: Includes the refundable security deposit. A deposit that must be returned is not income until the landlord keeps it.

items.topic: Reporting of items from pass-through entities
items.task: Use information from disregarded and pass-through entities to report an owner's share of ordinary business income (loss) and separately stated items on an individual's tax return.
items.stem: Rae Kim is the sole shareholder of Fern Inc., a calendar-year S corporation. Her stock basis is $0. She lent Fern $30,000 in exchange for a written note and has held the note for several years. Fern's losses in prior years reduced her basis in the note to $12,000. In 2026 Fern broke even (no income, loss, or distributions) and repaid the entire $30,000 note in cash. What is the effect of the repayment on Rae's 2026 return?
options: She recognizes no gain, because repayment of loan principal is a return of capital
She recognizes a $12,000 capital gain, the reduced basis in the note
She recognizes an $18,000 capital gain, because the repayment exceeds her reduced basis in the note
She reports $30,000 of ordinary income from the S corporation

why.A: Ignores the basis reduction. Repayment above the reduced basis is gain.
why.B: Uses the basis as the gain. Gain is the amount repaid less basis: $30,000 - $12,000.
why.C: Loss deductions reduced Rae's note basis to $12,000. Repayment of $30,000 exceeds it by $18,000, and there was no 2026 net increase to restore basis.
why.D: Repayment of the shareholder's own loan is not S corporation income. Only the amount exceeding basis is gain, and it is capital for a note.

steps: No net increase in 2026, so no restoration of note basis
Note held more than one year: long-term capital gain

items.stem: Gus and Lia each own an interest in a different calendar-year partnership that provides consulting services. Each 2026 Schedule K-1 shows $60,000 of ordinary business income and $30,000 of guaranteed payments for services the partner performed. Gus is a general partner. Lia is a limited partner who performs services for the partnership. Which statement correctly compares their 2026 net earnings from self-employment, before the 92.35% adjustment?

why.A: A general partner's distributive share and guaranteed payments are self-employment income: $60,000 + $30,000 = $90,000. A limited partner's distributive share is excluded, but guaranteed payments for services are included.
why.B: Excludes Lia's guaranteed payments as well. Only a limited partner's distributive share is excluded; payments for services are not.
why.C: Leaves out Gus's guaranteed payments. A general partner's guaranteed payments for services are self-employment income.
why.D: Treats the limited partner like a general partner. The distributive share of a limited partner is excluded.

steps: Limited partner: distributive share excluded; guaranteed payments 30,000

items.topic: Reporting of items from pass-through entities
items.task: Use information from disregarded and pass-through entities to report an owner's share of ordinary business income (loss) and separately stated items on an individual's tax return.
items.stem: Two partners each have a $22,000 basis in a partnership interest immediately before a current, non-liquidating distribution. Al receives $30,000 of cash. Bea receives land with a $30,000 fair market value and a $14,000 basis to the partnership. Assume no partnership liabilities and no unrealized receivables or inventory. Which statement correctly compares Al's and Bea's results?
options: Al recognizes no gain; Bea recognizes a $16,000 gain, the excess of fair market value over the partnership's basis
Al recognizes an $8,000 gain; Bea recognizes no gain, takes a $30,000 basis in the land, and has no remaining basis in her interest
Al and Bea each recognize an $8,000 gain, because each receives more than $22,000 of value
Al recognizes an $8,000 gain and has a $0 basis in his interest; Bea recognizes no gain, takes a $14,000 basis in the land, and has an $8,000 basis in her interest

why.A: Reverses the two results. A property distribution is not a taxable sale, and cash over basis is taxed.
why.B: Gives the land a fair market value basis. Basis is the partnership's basis, $14,000, limited to Bea's outside basis.
why.C: Gain is recognized on a current distribution of property only through cash exceeding basis. Bea receives no cash.
why.D: Cash over basis is gain to Al: $30,000 - $22,000. Property distributions carry over the partnership's basis ($14,000, limited to outside basis), and Bea's interest falls to $22,000 - $14,000 = $8,000.

steps: Bea: land basis = lesser of 14,000 or 22,000 = 14,000

items.topic: Reporting of items from pass-through entities

items.stem: Stan sold his entire interest in Harbor Partners, a cash-basis service partnership, for $100,000 in 2026. His basis in the interest was $60,000. Stan's share of the partnership's accounts receivable, which have a zero tax basis, is $15,000. The partnership has no inventory, collectibles, or depreciable real property. Which statement describes the character of Stan's total gain?
options: $25,000 of ordinary income and $15,000 of capital gain
$40,000 of capital gain, because a partnership interest is a capital asset
$15,000 of ordinary income and $25,000 of capital gain
$40,000 of ordinary income, because the partnership uses the cash method

why.A: Swaps the amounts. Only the portion attributable to the receivables is ordinary.
why.B: Ignores the look-through rule for unrealized receivables. That part of the amount realized is ordinary income.
why.C: Gain on the sale of a partnership interest is capital except to the extent attributable to unrealized receivables and inventory. The $15,000 receivable share is ordinary; the rest of the $40,000 gain is capital.
why.D: The cash method creates the zero-basis receivables but does not convert the whole gain to ordinary income.

items.task: Use information from disregarded and pass-through entities to report an owner's share of ordinary business income (loss) and separately stated items on an individual's tax return.
items.stem: Marsh Inc. is a calendar-year S corporation with two equal shareholders, Ori and Pam. Marsh earned $73,000 of ordinary business income in 2026, spread evenly at $200 per day for all 365 days. On June 30, 2026, Ori sold all his stock to Quinn. Marsh has no other classes of stock, made no distributions, and made no election to close its books. What ordinary income is reported on the 2026 Schedules K-1 of Ori, Pam, and Quinn, respectively?

why.A: Income is assigned equally to each day and split among the shares outstanding that day. The seller is treated as the shareholder on the day of sale. Ori: 181 days x $200 x 50% = $18,100. Quinn: 184 days x $200 x 50% = $18,400. Pam: $36,500.
why.B: Assigns the whole year's income to the shareholder at year end. Income is allocated by day among the shareholders during the year.
why.C: Splits the year evenly in half. The allocation uses actual days: 181 days through June 30 and 184 days from July 1.
why.D: Reverses the day counts. Ori owned through June 30, which is 181 days, and Quinn owned the remaining 184 days.

steps: January 1 through June 30 = 31+28+31+30+31+30 = 181 days; July 1 through December 31 = 184 days

items.task: Use information from disregarded and pass-through entities to report an owner's share of ordinary business income (loss) and separately stated items on an individual's tax return.
items.stem: Review the exhibit for Tom Ridge's 2026 return. Tom owns 40% of Ridge Supply Inc., an S corporation, and works there full time. His stock basis is ample. His draft return reports the $50,000 of ordinary business income on Schedule C, pays self-employment tax on it, and reports the $30,000 distribution as other income. Which correction is required?
exhibit: Stock basis at beginning of year
options: Keep the $50,000 on Schedule C because Tom works full time, but remove the $30,000 distribution from income
Report the $50,000 on Schedule E but keep the $30,000 distribution as dividend income
Report both the $50,000 and the $30,000 on Schedule E as ordinary income
Report the $50,000 on Schedule E, remove it from self-employment tax, and remove the $30,000 distribution from income because it does not exceed his basis

why.A: Working full time affects the reasonable wages the corporation must pay, not the character of pass-through income. It is not reported on Schedule C.
why.B: Treats a distribution from an S corporation with sufficient basis as a dividend. A distribution within basis is not taxed.
why.C: Adds the distribution to Schedule E income. The distribution reduces basis and is not income unless it exceeds basis.
why.D: S corporation ordinary income passes through on Schedule K-1 to Schedule E and is not self-employment income. A distribution up to stock basis is a nontaxable return of basis.

items.topic: Reporting of items from pass-through entities

items.stem: Fay Ott is a limited partner in Orchard LP. Her basis in the interest at the beginning of 2026 was $25,000, including her $22,000 share of partnership nonrecourse liabilities. During 2026 her share of partnership income was $6,000. The partnership repaid a nonrecourse loan, which reduced Fay's share of liabilities from $22,000 to $4,000, and it also distributed $20,000 of cash to her. There were no other adjustments. What gain does Fay recognize in 2026?

why.A: Counts only the $20,000 of cash actually received, which is less than her $31,000 basis. The liability decrease is also a deemed distribution.
why.B: Basis rises by income to $31,000. The $18,000 decrease in her liability share is a deemed cash distribution, so total distributions are $20,000 + $18,000 = $38,000. Gain is the excess over basis: $38,000 - $31,000 = $7,000.
why.C: Omits the $6,000 basis increase for her share of income, so the gain is overstated.
why.D: Treats the deemed distribution from the liability decrease as gain by itself. It is taxed only to the extent total distributions exceed basis.

items.stem: Jo Diaz contributed land with a $30,000 adjusted basis and a $50,000 fair market value to a partnership in exchange for a 50% interest. Kit contributed $50,000 cash for the other 50%. How much of the gain on the sale is allocated to Jo?

why.A: Assumes the sale at fair market value produces no gain. The partnership's basis in the land is Jo's $30,000, not $50,000.
why.B: Splits the gain equally under the agreement. Built-in gain at contribution is allocated to the contributing partner.
why.C: The partnership takes Jo's $30,000 basis, so it recognizes a $20,000 gain. The precontribution gain of $20,000 must be allocated entirely to Jo.
why.D: Takes 50% of the sale price instead of allocating the gain. Gain is price less the partnership's basis.

items.topic: Adjustments and deductions to AGI and taxable income
items.task: Review Form 1040 and supporting documentation to determine accuracy of AGI and taxable income reported.
items.stem: Sal and Tess Ward file jointly for 2026 and take the standard deduction. Their draft return claims a $2,000 charitable deduction for the gifts listed in the exhibit. What charitable deduction should they claim?
exhibit: Cash to their church (a public charity)
Cash to a donor-advised fund at a community foundation
Cash to a supporting organization of a local hospital
Used clothing given to a charity thrift shop (fair market value)

why.A: Applies the $1,000 limit for other filers. The joint return limit is $2,000, but the eligible gifts total only $1,500.
why.B: A taxpayer who does not itemize may deduct only cash gifts to qualifying public charities, up to $2,000 on a joint return. Gifts to a donor-advised fund, to a supporting organization, and noncash gifts do not count, leaving the $1,500 church gift.
why.C: Applies the joint return limit to gifts that include ineligible amounts. The deduction cannot exceed the eligible cash gifts of $1,500.
why.D: Counts all cash gifts ($1,500 + $900 + $600) without excluding the donor-advised fund and supporting organization gifts or applying the limit.

steps: Eligible cash gifts to public charities = 1,500 (fund, supporting organization, and noncash excluded)
items.law_note: OBBBA (P.L. 119-21 sec. 70424) added IRC 170(p): nonitemizers may deduct cash gifts to public charities up to $1,000 ($2,000 joint), taxable years beginning after 2025. Excluded: gifts to 509(a)(3) organizations and for donor-advised funds. Verified against Cornell LII 26 USC 170(p).

items.topic: Adjustments and deductions to AGI and taxable income
items.task: Calculate the qualified business income (QBI) deduction for federal income tax purposes.
items.stem: Rick Sloan, single, has two sole proprietorships, neither a specified service business. For 2026 his landscaping business had qualified business income of $90,000 and his food-truck business had a qualified business loss of $30,000. His taxable income before the qualified business income deduction is $140,000, below the threshold amount, and includes no net capital gain. What is his qualified business income deduction?

why.A: Qualified business income from all businesses is netted: $90,000 - $30,000 = $60,000. The deduction is 20% of $60,000 = $12,000, below the 20% of taxable income limit of $28,000.
why.B: Ignores the loss from the food-truck business. Losses reduce combined qualified business income.
why.C: Adds the loss instead of subtracting it.
why.D: Uses the taxable income limit as the deduction. The deduction is the lesser of 20% of net qualified business income and 20% of taxable income.

items.law_note: OBBBA made the section 199A deduction permanent for years after 2025. No phase-in computation is asked.

After correcting for the omission, what is the medical expense deduction?
exhibit: Medical deduction on the draft ($9,500 - 7.5% x $80,000)
Deductible IRA contribution omitted from the draft

why.D: Applies the corrected floor but adds an unrelated $1,000. Medical expenses above 7.5% of AGI are deductible, and nothing else adjusts the amount.
